topic: stochastic knapsack; generalized assignment; sparsification; exact-solver preprocessing
status: bounded evaluation lead from one sampled ITCS 2026 full text; novelty not established
claim: The sampled sparsifier has a formal near-optimality guarantee under its stochastic packing model and reports positive synthetic deterministic results, but practical gains are conditional on redundancy, bin count, instance size, and how quickly the full MILP solver exploits presolve/dominance. Its own established GAP benchmarks and hardness constructions are sparse, and a large n=10000,m=5 slice behaves anomalously because of generator-specific structure. The next evidence step is a controlled, solver-aware real-workload study, not a blanket practical-speedup claim.
positive_evidence: The paper proves dimension-independent polynomial-degree sparsification results for knapsack, multiple knapsack, and generalized assignment under independent activation and its stated polyhedral degree definition.

Its synthetic p=1 experiments report mean approximation ratio 0.998 and mean end-to-end speedup 2.79x over all runs; the filtered high-redundancy slice reports 4.67x speedup and 5.14x equal-time incumbent ratio.
The authors stratify by redundancy, bin count, correlation and size and explicitly diagnose the n=10000,m=5 behavior as data-generator-specific rather than relying on it for the main claim.
counterevidence: Established hard GAP constructions and existing GAP benchmark sets are reported by the authors to be sparse, limiting evidence on the intended redundancy regime.
The experiments are synthetic and deterministic (p=1), use practical parameters weaker than the theorem's worst-case settings, and do not establish transfer to operational data.
For easy/small or solver-friendly slices, preprocessing overhead can erase the benefit; runtime and quality are also sensitive to modern solver behavior.

sources.sections: Main theorem; Section 4.4 and Appendix B experimental protocol/results; conclusion

falsifiable_test: On operational packing/assignment instances with documented provenance and no label leakage, preserve capacities, item values, assignment-specific weights, and activation model while generating matched redundancy levels. Compare full MILP, sparsify-plus-MILP, and equal-wall-clock full MILP. Report objective ratio, optimality gap, end-to-end time, presolve reductions, memory, and failure rate by solver/version and instance strata. The lead weakens if speed/quality gains survive on naturally low-redundancy and solver-friendly cases; it strengthens if there is a stable, pre-registered threshold where redundancy predicts improvement. Not run here.
limitations: One paper, primarily synthetic p=1 evaluation, no reproduced experiment or actual industry dataset. The proposed test is not evidence of novelty and the theorem/model is narrower than arbitrary stochastic packing.

topic: speed scaling; weighted flow time; energy-aware scheduling; complexity classification
status: bounded theorem-registry status correction and approximation lead from one sampled STACS 2026 full text; novelty not established
claim: For the newly resolved speed-scaling variants, the phrase ‘the job order is known’ is insufficient: prescribed priority order still permits NP-hardness, while a prescribed completion-time order yields polynomial-time LP optimization. The paper also supplies counterexamples to two natural extensions of an earlier two-speed algorithm to k speeds. A reliable complexity registry must key results by objective, integral/fractional flow, continuous/discrete speed, weight/size regime, and order semantics; approximation of the NP-hard cases remains a separate question.
positive_evidence: The paper proves NP-hardness for four formerly open flow-plus-energy/energy-budget cases, including when schedules must follow a prescribed priority ordering.
Theorem 3 gives a polynomial-time LP approach when a completion-time ordering is supplied and identifies the ordering itself as a source of complexity.
The paper gives counterexamples to two natural k-speed generalizations of a prior two-speed algorithm, illustrating a concrete failed transfer across models.
counterevidence: These are worst-case classification results, not a statement that realistic speed-scaling scheduling is intractable to approximate or that no useful heuristics exist.
The paper cites an online (2+epsilon)-competitive algorithm for one NP-hard offline variant, so NP-hardness coexists with nontrivial approximation guarantees.
This audit checks one paper and does not exhaustively enumerate all later approximation or implementation literature.

sources.sections: Definitions; Theorems 1–3; Sections 3–5 counterexamples; Discussion and Future Work

falsifiable_test: For each theorem/algorithm record, audit the full tuple (objective, flow definition, speed domain, weights, job sizes, release model, supplied order type). Attempt to reproduce the two-speed extension on the paper's counterexample instances and compare it with the LP algorithm. For approximation leads, derive a ratio or hardness bound for the explicitly NP-hard variants under the same tuple. A mismatched tuple or counterexample falsifies any claim that a result transfers without qualification. Not run here.
limitations: One theoretical source; no schedule implementation, energy trace, or independent proof reconstruction. The approximation direction is broad and may be partly addressed by cited work.

topic: streaming algorithms; union-size estimation; Klee's measure; test coverage; DNF counting; formal verification
status: bounded implementation/evaluation lead from one sampled revised arXiv full text; novelty not established
claim: The 2026 revised union-estimation paper materially improves proof auditability by formalizing theorem statements and machine-checking correctness in Lean 4, while retaining a theoretically efficient insertion-only algorithm for Delphic set families. This does not itself verify end-to-end implementation cost: its guarantees depend on efficient membership/sampling/counting interfaces, and the improved test-coverage space algorithm uses an NP oracle. The bounded next question is which concrete test-coverage/KMP/DNF workloads can instantiate these interfaces efficiently and whether asymptotic update bounds survive actual oracle and representation costs.
positive_evidence: The paper formalizes Delphic sets and proves a streaming estimator with applications to discrete Klee's measure, combinatorial test coverage, and DNF model counting.
The 2026 revision explicitly reports fixing prior proof typos/bugs, formalizing theorem statements, and machine-checking the proofs in Lean 4.

The paper states concrete asymptotic time/space guarantees, distinguishes a base algorithm from an NP-oracle-assisted space improvement, and identifies broader generalization/turnstile/higher-moment questions.
counterevidence: The revised arXiv text says the main claims remain unchanged; its proof correction note does not by itself imply the published result was false.
The insertion-only and Delphic-oracle restrictions may exclude realistic dynamic workloads; NP-oracle update-time accounting is not ordinary executable runtime.
No implementation benchmark or deployment evidence is provided in the sampled full text, and practical query costs can dominate asymptotic update bounds.

sources.sections: Abstract revision note; Theorem 1.6; Corollaries 1.7/1.10/1.12; Theorem 1.11; conclusion

falsifiable_test: Implement APS-Estimator on one concrete workload from each claimed application and compare to established union/F0 baselines on identical insertion-only streams. Include actual membership/sampling/counting oracle latency, per-update p50/p95, memory, oracle calls, and (epsilon,delta) empirical coverage; separately report proof/formalization and runtime results. Extend to deletions only with a separately stated model and correctness argument. The lead weakens if oracle overhead is negligible and the published asymptotic costs already predict wall-clock behavior; it strengthens if interface costs or stream deletions erase the gains. Not run here.
limitations: One revised theory paper; implementation work, benchmarks, and exhaustive follow-up search were not performed. Lean proof does not guarantee executable efficiency or correctness of an unrelated implementation.
